Keep 'officials suspect' wording for the GLP-1 link, and give 2026 as a 'so far' year-to-date figure. Frame it as protecting the people who collect your trash, with no shaming. Exact prescriber line. Cut to 35–50s.

package.description:
NYC sanitation workers reported 49 needle-stick injuries in 2026 through August, and 140 over the past 3 years. The department says it may be linked to more people using injectable GLP-1s (semaglutide, tirzepatide); doctors say insulin and other injectables are part of the picture too. Here's how to dispose of used pens and needles safely.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Your trash crew can get hurt by pens and needles tossed loose. 💉

NYC sanitation workers reported 49 needle-stick injuries in 2026 (through August) — and 140 over the past 3 years, per the city's sanitation department. Officials say rising injectable GLP-1 use (semaglutide, tirzepatide — like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro) may be part of it. Doctors say insulin and other injectables are part of the picture too.

Used pen needles, single-dose pens and syringes are all sharps — never loose in trash or recycling.

✅ Once it's about three-quarters full, seal it and follow your local rules — drop-off, mail-back, or household trash where allowed.

factcheck.summary: I checked every number and claim against the linked sources, and they hold up. CBS New York (20 Aug 2026) reports 49 DSNY needle-stick injuries in 2026 as of 10 Aug. ABC7 (24 Aug 2026) reports 140 over the past three years. ABC7 also carries the department's hedged line that the rise "may be linked" to GLP-1 needles. CBS covers the note from healthcare professionals that insulin, EpiPens and fertility injectables are also common. The FDA pages support each disposal step: auto-injector pens count as sharps, an FDA-cleared container or a heavy-duty plastic household container with a tight-fitting, puncture-resistant lid, labelled, about three-quarters full, then follow local rules, including household trash only where the state allows. SafeNeedleDisposal.org (a NeedyMeds project) does list disposal rules by state. The prescriber line is there word for word, and there's no dosing or medication-change advice. Five small wording fixes are listed below: a small logic slip in the loop ending, pen-scope wording on screen, an unsupported "30-second" claim, a source tag, and one balancing hedge.

issues.claim: Do this, and 49 gets smaller. / Help 49 get smaller
issues.problem: 49 is a running year-to-date count, so it can only go up during 2026. As written, the promise can't be true.
issues.fix: Narration: "It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you. Do this, and fewer crews become the next 49." On-screen: "Fewer crews in the next 49"

issues.problem: This is broader than the narration and the sources. Pen needles, single-dose pens (autoinjectors) and syringes are sharps. For multi-dose pens like Ozempic, the guidance on the empty pen body varies (Novo Nordisk says sharps container; some local guidance allows trash once the needle is removed). On-screen text shouldn't claim more than the narration does.
None of the sources gives a time figure. It's a made-up number that reads like a fact.

issues.claim: 140 in the past three years, per the city's sanitation department.
issues.problem: The 140 figure appears only in ABC7 (v1). CBS (v2) gives yearly figures (18 in 2020, 46 in 2025, 49 in 2026) instead.
issues.fix: Tag the 140 on-screen line to v1 only: set the s2 stat source to "ABC7 / DSNY" and keep v2 for the doctors/insulin sentence.

issues.claim: The department says it may be linked to more people using injectable GLP-1s.
issues.problem: CBS reports that DSNY cannot confirm which needle types are causing the injuries. Adding that keeps the causal framing honest.
issues.fix: "The department says it may be linked to more people using injectable GLP-1s, though it can't confirm which needles. Doctors say insulin and other injectables are part of the picture too."
